summary: A framework from SRI-ARC for coordinating the surveys and data-gathering efforts about network resources, the Resource Notebook. The goals were to avoid swamping sites with overlapping questionnaires and to make the NIC responsible for coordination. ARPA had agreed to the scheme.

plainLanguage.summary: Too many people were sending surveys to the same computer sites, so one office was chosen to collect the answers for everyone.

questions: what was the nic's role in the arpanet
subtitle: A 1973 plan to make the Network Information Center the single coordinator of surveys about network resources.

tldr.problem: Several groups were running their own surveys to collect "resource notebook" information, which risked overwhelming the sites and people who had to answer them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes that the Network Information Center (NIC) coordinate collecting, verifying and disseminating the data, helped by regional data collectors, and that a working group review the situation periodically.
tldr.outcome: It was a proposal with ARPA's agreement, offered for comment by March 9; the text does not say what came of it.

today: The status in the unit data is Unknown and no obsoleting or updating documents are recorded. It remains a historical record of how ARPANET resource information was to be organized.

sections.title: The Problem and the Two Goals
sections.content:
The RFC presents a framework for coordinating all the surveys and data-gathering efforts concerned with resource notebook information. The author says agreement from ARPA had already been obtained.

The scheme has two purposes: to avoid a proliferation of data-gathering efforts that would overwhelm the sites and people supplying the information, and to give the NIC responsibility for coordinating the tasks of the resource notebook. Two companion documents, NIC 14514 (the history of the notebook from 1971) and NIC 14515 (the questionnaire the NIC was sending to server sites), give more detail.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone asks the same people the same questions, those people get tired. So one office will ask once.

sections.title: The Framework
sections.content:
The NIC would coordinate collecting, verifying and disseminating the data. Because of the size of the task, regional data collectors would help both the NIC and the supplying sites. Initially there would be five regions: Boston, Washington DC, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Mid-Continent.

Each regional agent would gather information from sites in the region and forward it to the NIC for the Resource Notebook data base, with the NIC working closely with them to keep the data accurate and up to date.

For dissemination, different subsets or "views" of the information were needed. Whoever prepared them, the views should be available on-line at the NIC as well as off-line. A working group would meet periodically to review the situation and make concrete proposals.
sections.plainLanguage: Helpers in five parts of the country collect the answers and send them to the main office, which keeps one big, tidy list that others can look at.

sections.title: Discussion and Related Work
sections.content:
The RFC invites discussion and offers a meeting at SRI-ARC, suggested for Monday March 19, 1973, at 8:30 AM, with comments requested by March 9.

It also notes that a recent RFC by John Iseli and Dave Crocker (RFC 462) addresses the same problem area but proposes a different framework for data collection.
sections.plainLanguage: The author asks for opinions and mentions that two other people had a different plan for the same job.

references.text: Iseli, J. and Crocker, D., NWG/RFC 462, NIC 14434.
